Some residents impacted by the Norte Fire, which has burnt up to 570 acres in San Clemente and San Juan Capistrano , are now able to return to their homes, after about thousands of residents were under evacuation orders and warnings yesterday.
In a midday update, OC Sheriff Department and OC Fire Authorities spokespeople announced some evacuation zones have reopened, meaning that residents in those areas can return home.
Evacuation orders in Zone 13 in Northern San Clemente have been fully lifted, while evacuation orders have partially been lifted in Zone 10 in San Juan Capistrano for only the Stallion Ridge Community, San Juan Hills High School and the Prima Deschecha landfill.
“Other evacuation orders are still in effect, and that's due to the fact that we do have an active fire line, we do have wind, and we have a heat advisory in effect so there is still a risk,” said Greg Barta, a spokesman for the Orange County Fire Authority.
For a map of the evacuation zones,   click here .
Road closures are still in effect.
“We maintain road closures in all other areas and we encourage people to stay out of the area as crews continue to keep the community safe,” said Lizbeth Gwisdalla, a spokeswoman for the OC Sheriff’s department, in a video posted to X this afternoon.
OC Fire Authority officials said they contained about 5% of the fire overnight in a Saturday morning update.
“Our actions today will be to continue to attack the fire and work towards getting residents home as soon as it’s safe to do so,” said Barta in a video posted to X this morning.
Gwisdalla said Saturday morning about 16,000 residents and 6,000 structures were under evacuation orders.
It was also announced this morning that the affected areas will be receiving funding from the Federal Emergency Management Agency , or FEMA, to support the fire fighting.

Mandatory evacuation orders are in place for San Juan Zones 4, 5, and 10, alongside neighboring San Clemente Zones 12 and 13 according to social media posts from the OC Fire Authority, who also noted structures are threatened.

Evacuation centers are open at the San Juan Capistrano Community Center 25925 Camino del Avion, San Juan Capistrano and San Clemente Community Center 100 Calle Seville, San Clemente.
Nine schools have gone into early dismissal and are asking parents to pick up their children immediately according to the OC Department of Education, including Bernice Ayer Middle School, Clarence Lobo Elementary School, Concordia Elementary School, Harold Ambuehl Elementary School, San Clemente High School, San Juan Hills High School, Shorecliffs Middle School, Truman Benedict Elementary School and Vista Del Mar.
As of 4:22 pm, OC Fire Authority announced six homes had been “damaged or destroyed,” by the fire, noting the blaze was still at over 450 acres.
The blaze, dubbed the Norte Fire, was first reported at around 11:30 in the area of Portico Del Norte according to the Orange County Fire Authority, a street in San Clemente near the landfill.

https://voiceofoc.org/2026/10/rynerson-o.title: Rynerson: Orange County Power Authority Offers Both More Choice and More Transparency than Southern California Edison
https://voiceofoc.org/2026/10/rynerson-o.text:
A number of people have questioned whether or not the Orange County Power Authority (OCPA) actually gets its power from the green sources that it claims to: solar, wind, and hydroelectric. They also suggest that OCPA forces consumers onto their most expensive 100% Renewable rate plan. In short, an assertion that OCPA is less than transparent and that it is taking advantage of consumers. A little research can clearly debunk these assertions.
Let’s take the rate plan issue first. When a city opts in to use OCPA that city has a choice what rate will be the default rate for their constituents. When Huntington Beach, where I live, opted in, the default plan was Smart Choice – OCPA’s mid-tier offering. An offering that, at that time was actually less expensive than SCE’s standard rate. And, importantly, every subscriber could choose to either accept the default plan, or to choose any of the three plans that OCPA offered: Basic Choice, Smart Choice, or 100% Renewable. In fact, each subscriber could even choose to opt out of OCPA altogether and stay with SCE. So, the choice of plan is 100% in the hands of each individual subscriber. This information was communicated to all ratepayers in every bill for about three months prior to the transition, along with a simple web site where each user could record their choice. So, if each city chooses what they want to be the default rate plan, and each ratepayer can easily override that decision and pick any plan they want, doesn’t it seem ludicrous to claim that OCPA is forcing all users onto the most expensive plan?

https://voiceofoc.org/2026/10/man-violen.title: Man Violently Arrested by Santa Ana Police Speaks Up
https://voiceofoc.org/2026/10/man-violen.text:
Florentino Lopez said he woke up from a nap on Oct. 1, showered and stepped outside his home to smoke marijuana after working at his dad’s landscaping job before Santa Ana police officers called him over, leading to his violent arrest.
Lopez, a 28-year-old Santa Ana resident on probation in part for carrying a loaded firearm, said the police car drove by the house, then reversed and he recognized one of the officers calling him over as Luis Casillas – an officer who Lopez said often drives by and jokes with him – and complied with the request.
That's when, Lopez said, the officers came out of the car and a verbal argument kicked off before they bent him over against the hood of the car as his sister and later other family members stepped out of the house and started to record.
What happened next was caught on camera – one of the officers threw Lopez from the car onto the street and began to punch him repeatedly in the head before the second officer joined in and held Lopez’s legs down until more officers showed up " ostensibly to help restrain him.
“I still think it was a dream. It happened so quick,” Lopez said in an interview outside his home Thursday evening, recounting his Oct. 1 arrest. “I should have just stayed sleeping, man.”
“I was just shocked. I didn't feel shit. I was numbed,” he continued. “I trip out still to this today – getting kneed, getting all that.”
Lopez said he was surprised by the officers’ behavior because he knew Casillas and had interacted with him several times and said they were respectful with each other, adding it seemed like the officers were out looking to mess with someone.
Videos filmed of the arrest by his family would go viral on Instagram in the days after, sparking calls for accountability in a town where local officials often face scrutiny and concerns over police using excessive force but rarely have public discussions about police accountability.

https://voiceofoc.org/2026/10/newport-be.text:
Newport Beach leaders are looking to beef up their shoreline protections from coastal flooding ahead of an expected super El Niño after much of the Balboa Peninsula flooded last weekend, with leaders discussing sand replenishment opportunities and other protections.
“There’s a lot of ideas out there, it just costs money,” Councilmember Erik Weigand said during Tuesday’s meeting, adding, “We have to figure out how to pay for it all, but I do think it's something that we need to do.”
City Manager Seimone Jurjis said the city’s sand berms will be maintained as long as possible, potentially until January after high tides subside. In addition, city staff will also monitor and maintain flood reduction measures and storm water pumping operations.
During a presentation on beach management efforts from last weekend’s flooding from Storm Rachel, Public Works Director Dave Webb warned the city of king tides on Oct. 26 and in late November and December, El Niño and the Kelvin wave.
Newport Beach on Oct. 10, 2026. JULIE LEOPO, Voice of OC
Webb also said residents must also do their part by reusing sand bags, raising their private sea walls, avoiding driving in flooded streets, and moving cars and personal property to higher ground.
“This is a self-help city, you can’t expect the government is going to solve all of this,” Webb said.
But dozens of residents also pointed out they need the city to take the lead in a disaster.
“At a certain point, there is only so much the residents can do,” said resident Jack Grace during public comment. “I can only fill up so many sand bags.”
Walter Stahr, a candidate for city council, was one of several residents who questioned whether city leaders did enough to prepare for the disaster in the first place.

https://voiceofoc.org/2026/10/lawsuit-ac.text:
A civil lawsuit alleging an Orange County Board of Education trustee attacked a 20-year-old driver, throwing him to the ground and choking him, has been dismissed after the driver’s lawyers moved to drop the case.
The lawsuit was filed in 2024 and recounts an alleged road rage incident from 2023 involving OC Board of Education Trustee Ken Williams Jr., who issued a statement through his lawyers to Voice of OC on Wednesday.
“For his part, Dr. Williams has always disputed Mr. O’Malley’s version of events,” wrote David Libman, Williams’ attorney.
Court filings claimed that Williams was driving down a residential road in Silverado when Caden O’Malley approached in his vehicle from behind.
Original filings also claimed that Williams slammed on his brakes multiple times in front of O’Malley’s vehicle before they both pulled over and exited their vehicles.
O’Malley claimed that when he approached Williams’ Escalade to take a picture of the license plate, Williams allegedly rushed at him, threw him to the ground, climbed on top of him and started choking him while O’Malley pleaded for him to stop — according to the original complaint filed in court.
On July 13, counsel for O’Malley filed a request for the entire case to be dismissed with prejudice. The Orange County Superior Court entered the dismissal that same day.
That means the case has been permanently closed, and O’Malley cannot file the same lawsuit again.
“Reporting on this lawsuit has seemed to rely heavily on Mr. O’Malley’s unproven allegations without much consideration of Dr. Williams’ side of the story,” Libman wrote. “Dr. Williams has always maintained that he was acting in self-defense and that Mr. O’Malley was acting as the aggressor.”
“To settle this dispute, the parties entered an agreement in June 2026 in exchange for a mutual release of claims; no money was exchanged,” Libman added.
O’Malley’s attorney declined to comment in a Thursday morning email to Voice of OC.

https://voiceofoc.org/2026/10/huntington.text:
Spending is heating up in the race for Huntington Beach City Council after the local police officer’s association dropped nearly $100,000 in independent advertising targeting sitting council members who voted against their raises and supporting their opponents.
The Huntington Beach Police Officers Association has spent over $100,000 on city council races as of Oct. 13 according to campaign disclosures.
Most of that spending came through the police union’s political action committee, where they disclosed spending $16,000 apiece opposing Mayor Casey McKeon and Councilman Pat Burns just weeks after they voted against a nearly 18% raise for officers over the next three years.
They also spent over $17,000 on ads supporting Councilman Andrew Gruel’s candidacy after he voted in favor of the raises, and donated an additional $5,900 directly to Gruel’s campaign accounts.
The police union also spent another $17,000 on advertising candidate Brian Burley and endorsed him, as well as an additional $31,000 in advertising on Taryn Palumbo and Erin Spivey’s candidacy combined.
They’re the largest independent group spending on the race, with the Manufactured Housing Educational Trust Political Action Committee, largely funded by mobile home park owners, spending $15,000 combined advertising McKeon, Gruel, Burns and candidate Brian Thienes.
While the police union’s political action committee is spending big heading into the Nov. 3 election, one city council candidate is throwing over a quarter of a million dollars of his own money into his campaign accounts and several challengers out-fundraising the sitting mayor this year.
All the money is flowing into a city council race with 11 candidates vying for four seats to shape Surf City’s future after spending the last four years becoming one of the loudest voices opposing state legislators and endorsing local control.

The Orange County District Attorney’s office has decided to drop criminal charges against Florentino Lopez, a man beaten by two Santa Ana police officers at the start of the month in a violent arrest captured on a viral video.
“Based on the totality of the evidence in the case, including the body worn camera video, we determined that pursuing the probation violation was the most appropriate sanction,” reads a statement from Kimberly Edds, a spokeswoman for the District Attorney’s office, Wednesday.
John Kremer, Lopez’s attorney, said he was surprised the case was suddenly dismissed, adding that Lopez is happy the charges were dropped.
“Unfortunately, there is going to be a probation violation hearing in December, based primarily on the charges that were in the prior felony case that was dismissed. So we're still going to have to fight the case, but in a different format,” Kremer said in a Wednesday phone interview.
“The video is pretty clear what happened, it speaks for itself and I think they realize that – that may be one reason the prosecutors dropped the case because of the video and the public outcry.”
The decision to drop the charges comes weeks after a video went viral of Lopez’s Oct. 1 arrest showing Lopez bent over the front hood of a police car arguing with police officers before one officer throws him onto the street and begins to punch him repeatedly in the head.
A second officer then joins in and holds Lopez’s legs down before two more police officers show up and help restrain him.
According to his Oct. 5 criminal complaint , Lopez was charged with resisting arrest, smoking marijuana near a school, day care or youth center and unlawfully blocking the roadway as a result of the incident. He pleaded not guilty to the charges.
Lopez is currently on probation for a hit-and-run, carrying a loaded gun and reckless driving.

https://voiceofoc.org/2026/10/anaheim-po.title: Anaheim Police Get $45 Million Raise Ahead of $120 Million in Freed Up Bond Money
https://voiceofoc.org/2026/10/anaheim-po.text:
Without any public discussion, Anaheim officials approved a nearly 17% wage hike for police officers over the next three years as part of a new contract with the police union that will cost city taxpayers $45 million.
The approval comes months after city officials warned this year’s budget deficit would eat up nearly half of the $120 million in new revenue expected to be freed up after the 1997 Disneyland Resort expansion bonds are paid off early.
Yet Anaheim City Council members unanimously voted for the pay raise without any public discussion on Tuesday as part of the consent calendar – a block of items typically covering routine city business, like tree trimming, that’s voted on simultaneously.
It also comes as a host of labor contracts are expected to be up for renewal this year and next – increased costs that city officials have not taken into account in their positive financial projections for the next five years.
City Spokesman Mike Lyster said the cost of the contract will be covered by “available resources” within the budget including potentially from reserves or the freed up revenue from the bond.

https://voiceofoc.org/2026/10/will-orang.text:
Editor’s Note: This questionnaire is part of an ongoing series publishing candidates’ opinions on how they would run the government if they were elected county supervisor. All questionnaires are archived on the Voice of OC Elections Page .
Orange County Supervisors have faced growing questions over the past year about their use of discretionary funds as they start to dwindle down.
The funds were launched during the COVID-19 pandemic, but supervisors have continued to spend them for years after lockdowns were lifted, awarding hundreds of thousands of dollars to handpicked community organizations, nonprofits and events in their districts.
They only beefed up disclosure of where that money was going after a public scandal involving former Supervisor Andrew Do, who used some of his funds to illegally support a nonprofit his daughter worked at , crimes which he later went to prison for.
We asked candidates for county supervisor if they would support making those discretionary funds permanent or not.
Would you support an effort to expand or replenish county supervisors’ discretionary budgets?
Dixon , Fifth District : I would not support expanding discretionary budgets under the current system. With the county facing a structural budget imbalance, any additional spending needs to be carefully justified. The Andrew Do scandal also showed why stronger safeguards are needed when individual supervisors control taxpayer dollars. There are worthwhile community organizations and local needs that deserve county support, but taxpayers should be able to see where that money goes, why it was awarded and how it was ultimately spent.
Foley, Fifth District : We must address the County’s structural budget imbalance, obtain a third-party independent audit of the county financials, and protect essential services before considering additional discretionary funding for supervisors.

https://voiceofoc.org/2026/10/tustin-pol.title: Tustin Police to Get Access to School Camera Feeds Amid Growing Surveillance Concerns
https://voiceofoc.org/2026/10/tustin-pol.text:
Tustin police officers are set to get access to certain cameras in local schools in an attempt to improve awareness and response times during emergencies or threats of violence.
It’s part of a partnership between the Tustin Unified School District and the Tustin Police Department that was approved by city council members during a meeting last month. Officers are expected to get the camera feed access by the end of the year.
It comes at a time when a host of residents across Orange County are growing increasingly concerned about surveillance cameras intruding on people's privacy rights.
That’s especially true for automated license plate reader devices known as Flock cameras that record driver’s license plates and store the information in a database that police officers can access when investigating crimes.
Scores of residents across the county and nation have spoken out against the devices, claiming they don’t want their movements tracked and recorded.
The City of Fullerton was the first in OC to put a pause on their use of Flock cameras for the next six months to see what it will be like without them. The Tustin Police Department also uses Flock cameras .
Tustin City Council members unanimously approved an agreement during a Sept. 1 meeting that establishes guidelines for connecting selected schools’ surveillance cameras to the police department’s public safety technology platform.
“The [agreement] allows Tustin PD to access the TUSD camera system for situational awareness and to inform responses to active threats,” Tustin Mayor Austin Lumbard wrote in an email to Voice of OC.
The partnership would authorize Tustin police officers to have access to surveillance cameras during situations when they are aware of an emergency at a school or if a 911 call is received.
Lumbard said that the partnership can serve as an additional layer to enhance the safety and security of students and staff.

https://voiceofoc.org/2026/10/coastal-er.title: Coastal Erosion Partially Shuts Down PCH in Laguna Beach
https://voiceofoc.org/2026/10/coastal-er.text:
One southbound lane of the Pacific Coast Highway running between El Moro and Irvine Cove has closed after a large crack appeared on the side of a bluff which supports the highway near Laguna Beach.
It comes after the past weekend’s high tides and strong waves battered coastal Orange County towns, even flooding places like Balboa Peninsula in Newport Beach and streets in Laguna Beach.
While the state highway is not in Laguna Beach’s jurisdiction, the city released a video on Instagram Tuesday afternoon detailing the damage and expected delays.
“We reached out to CalTrans and they did confirm that the closure is related to some potential issues in the shoulder of the road,” said Tom Perez, Laguna Beach public works and utilities director, in the Instagram video.
“We have no information as far as how deep or what the extent of the crack is, but CalTrans is working on investigating the issue and determining what course of action they may need to take for any repairs.”
Currently, there is no estimated reopening date, and traffic will likely be affected for several days.
“We don’t know how long this will last, it will depend on their analysis of what has gone wrong there, but it will impact your day,” said City Manager Dave Kiff in the Instagram video.
Tropical Storm Rachel and unusually high tides brought surface flooding to several coastal cities in OC , with Newport Beach declaring a state of emergency after Balboa Peninsula was flooded Friday.
OC Supervisor Katrina Foley, who represents much of South OC, said the coast is already being impacted ahead of major storms or flooding from the expected super El Niño.
“Orange County is already experiencing serious coastal erosion as we prepare for the escalating impacts of a historic El Niño winter, and the storm season has yet to begin,” Foley said in a Tuesday afternoon news release.

https://voiceofoc.org/2026/10/company-be.text:
OC District Attorney Todd Spitzer and GKN Aerospace have come to a $125 million settlement agreement in the civil case against the company for a chemical tank that nearly exploded in Garden Grove in May – forcing 50,000 OC residents to evacuate their homes.
The agreement comes after GKN and the DA announced a $100 million claims program for residents and businesses in August affected by the hazmat incident, which is set to open this month .
“The civil case was filed in Orange County Superior Court today with the civil complaint along with the terms of the stipulated agreement,” reads an Oct. 12 news release from Spitzer’s office.
In addition to the $100 million claims program the company had already committed to, GKN will be paying out nearly $8.5 million for the emergency services that responded to the incident and pay an additional $15 million in civil penalties.
GKN will also pay $1.4 million for an outside organization to oversee their operations and undertake a “robust safety and monitoring plan” for seven years.
“The stipulated agreement marks an important milestone in the District Attorney’s Office’s efforts to recoup millions of dollars in taxpayer funds spent responding to the Memorial Day weekend hazmat incident by the County of Orange, the Orange County Fire Authority, and the cities of Garden Grove, Cypress, Stanton, Westminster, and Anaheim as well as the United States Environmental Protection Agency and the South Coast Air Quality Management District,” the news release reads.
Over Memorial Day weekend, residents in Garden Grove, Stanton and surrounding cities were evacuated after a chemical tank at GKN Aerospace hit dangerously high pressure , with fire officials at the time expecting it to either leak or explode.
Eventually, the tank was stabilized and evacuation orders ended on May 26.

https://voiceofoc.org/2026/10/oc-water-d.text:
Correction: An earlier version of this story incorrectly stated the OC Water District’s view that they were not allowed under their streambed alteration agreement with the state to disturb or remove any sediment in the Santa Ana River or vegetation growing in it. Officials say their reading of the agreement does allow those activities. We regret the error.
OC Water District’s efforts to keep bulldozing critical bird habitat along the Santa Ana River is drawing intense opposition from concerned residents and activists.
Last week, OC Water District’s Board of Directors were met with a dozen public commenters concerned about wildlife being harmed by the work happening on the river – with heavy equipment being brought in to tear out plant life growing in the stream.
The controversy comes after Creek Team activists effectively stopped OC Public Works from their continued use of herbicides in the county’s rivers and creeks. Now they are fighting to keep bird habitat on the Santa Ana River from being bulldozed and taken out by OC Water District.
Water district General Manager John Kennedy explained during the board of directors recent meeting how the work being done is in preparation for the winter season to help capture millions of dollars of water to be sold to cities around the county.
The Santa Ana River and its connecting channel on Oct. 9, 2026. Credit: SARA LEON, Voice of OC
“The district has been doing this work for many years to help keep the river and our recharge facilities ready to capture and recharge water when it becomes available. Heavy equipment, including bulldozers, is used for some of this work,” Kennedy said during last week’s meeting.
“We schedule this work outside the primary bird nesting season.”
However, the district received a recent violation in July from the California Department of Fish & Wildlife for illegally bulldozing a migratory bird nest in the Santa Ana River – which the water district is currently contesting.
